name: Design an Error Tracking Service
intent: Collect crashes and exceptions from millions of apps, turn a flood of raw events into a short list of distinct issues with readable stack traces, and tell the right team when something new or something old comes back.
finalIntro: One exception in a minified web app, from the browser to a Slack alert.
prompt: Design an error tracking service like Sentry. Developers add an SDK to their web, mobile and backend apps. Every unhandled exception is sent to the service, grouped with the same bug, shown with a readable stack trace, and counted. Teams get alerts for new issues, for old issues that come back after a fix, and for sudden spikes. One broken release must not take the service down or flood the team.
functional: An SDK captures exceptions, with breadcrumbs, release and user context, and sends them in batches
Group events that come from the same bug into one issue, and count them
Turn minified stack traces back into original file names, functions and lines using source maps
Mark an issue resolved, and detect a regression when it happens again in a later release
Alert on new issues, regressions and spikes, with rules per project
Enforce a quota and a rate limit per project, and sample or drop the excess
Keep events for a retention period, then delete them
nonFunctional: Accept an event in under 100 ms and never slow down or crash the customer's app
Handle a billion events per day, with peaks several times higher when a release breaks
An alert about a new issue reaches the team within about a minute
One noisy project must not delay or drop events of the others
Grouping is stable: the same bug stays in the same issue across releases
Keep source maps and events private to the owning organisation

firstAttempt.text: The SDK sends each exception as its own HTTP request to one API server, which inserts a row into an events table. An issue is a group of rows with the same error message. A cron job counts rows per message and emails the team when a count is high.
limits: Every error costs a request and a database write, so a crash loop in one app sends thousands of requests a second
Grouping by message splits one bug into many issues when the message holds an id or a number, and merges different bugs that share a message
Stack traces from minified code show names like a.b at line 1, so nobody can read them
One bad release in one project overloads the shared database for everyone
A cron job finds problems minutes late, and cannot tell a new bug from an old one that came back

steps.title: Capture in an SDK that batches and never hurts the app
steps.problem: Sending one request per error turns a crash loop into a denial of service against ourselves, and a slow error service must never slow down the app it watches.
steps.fix: A small SDK installs global handlers for uncaught exceptions and rejected promises. For each error it records the stack, the release, the environment and a trail of breadcrumbs, such as the last clicks and requests. Events go into an in-memory buffer and are sent asynchronously in a batch, after a few seconds or when about thirty events have collected. The SDK compresses the batch, uses a short timeout, backs off with jitter when the server answers 429 or 5xx, and drops events when its buffer is full. It can also sample, for example sending one in ten events of a very noisy kind, and it never throws.
steps.tradeoff: One request carries many events, the app is never blocked, and a crash loop is flattened at the source. Events can be lost if the page closes before the batch is sent, so the SDK also flushes on page hide with a beacon, and a hard native crash is written to disk and sent on the next start.

steps.title: Accept quickly at the edge, with a quota per project
steps.problem: Running grouping and storage inside the request means a spike makes every request slow, and one project in a crash loop can use all the capacity.
steps.fix: A thin ingest tier authenticates the public key in the project's DSN, checks the size and format, and applies the project's limits: a token bucket for the short-term rate and a monthly quota for the total. Accepted batches are written to a durable queue partitioned by project and the service answers 200 at once. Over the limit, it answers 429 with a Retry-After header, and the SDK stops sending for that time. Rejected events are still counted, so the dashboard can say how many were dropped.
steps.tradeoff: Ingest stays fast and cheap, and a noisy project hits its own limit, not the others'. The client key is public, so the limit is the main protection against abuse, and events are processed a few seconds after they are accepted, not inside the request.

steps.title: Fingerprint events and group them into issues
steps.problem: Ten thousand events from one bug must become one issue, and they differ in message, user, line number and timing.
steps.fix: Workers read the queue and compute a fingerprint: a hash of the exception type and the top few in-app stack frames, using file and function but not line numbers, and leaving out frames from libraries. When there is no stack, the fingerprint uses the message with numbers and ids replaced by a placeholder. The worker looks the fingerprint up in the issues database, creates the issue if it is new, and otherwise increments its counters, updates the last-seen release and time, and adds the event to the event store. Teams can override the rule with custom fingerprints or merge two issues by hand.
steps.tradeoff: Events from the same bug land in the same issue even when ids and line numbers change between releases. Any rule is a guess: too specific floods the team with duplicates, and too loose hides a second bug inside an old issue. Changing the rule later would split existing issues, so it is versioned.

steps.title: Symbolicate with source maps before fingerprinting
steps.problem: Production code is minified, so a stack shows a.b at bundle.js line 1 column 48210, and the names change with every release, which would split every issue at each deploy.
steps.fix: The build uploads the source maps for each release, keyed by release and file, to a private store. A symbolicator runs before fingerprinting: for each frame it finds the map for the event's release, looks up the line and column, and replaces them with the original file, function and lines, plus a few lines of source context. Parsed maps are kept in a cache, since thousands of events share the same few. Native crashes work the same way with debug symbol files, and a missing map leaves the frame as it was.
steps.tradeoff: Traces are readable, and fingerprints use original names, so one bug stays one issue across releases. Maps are large and must be uploaded on every release, the symbolicator needs memory and a cache, and a release without maps gives unreadable and badly grouped events until the maps arrive.

steps.title: Track issue state, detect regressions and alert
steps.problem: Teams do not want to read a list of thousands of issues. They want to hear about a bug that is new, a bug they fixed that came back, or a sudden increase.
steps.fix: Every issue has a state: unresolved, resolved, or ignored, and resolving can record the release that holds the fix. If an event arrives for a resolved issue from that release or a later one, the issue becomes regressed and an alert fires. Alert rules per project combine a trigger such as a new issue, a regression, or more than 200 events in 10 minutes, with filters such as the environment or the tag, and an action such as Slack, email or a pager. A rule fires once per issue per interval, to avoid repeating itself, and new issues are linked to the release that introduced them.
steps.tradeoff: People are told about what changed, and release health becomes visible within a minute of a deploy, which is a good gate for a canary. Rules need tuning, an old release still in use can look like a regression, and spike rules need a baseline to avoid waking the team for normal daily patterns.

steps.title: Sample hot issues and delete by retention
steps.problem: A billion events a day, kept for ninety days, is hundreds of terabytes, and most of it is the same few errors repeated millions of times.
steps.fix: Counters are exact and cheap, but full events are kept selectively. Once an issue passes a threshold in an hour, the service stores only a sample of its events, for example one in ten, and then one in a hundred, while the issue keeps counting everything. The event store is partitioned by day, so retention is dropping a partition after 30 or 90 days by plan, and the issue row, with its counters and first and last seen, lives much longer. Large payloads such as attachments go to cheaper object storage with their own lifetime.
steps.tradeoff: Storage cost follows the number of distinct problems, not the size of a loop, and deletion costs almost nothing. Sampled events mean a rare detail may be missing from the sample, and users must understand that the count is exact while the stored events are examples.

failures.scenario: A bad release puts an app in a crash loop and sends 100,000 events a second
failures.impact: Without limits this fills the queue and delays the events and alerts of every project.
failures.answer: The SDK buffer and its sampling limit what leaves the device, then the project's token bucket answers 429 and the SDK pauses. Queue partitions are per project, so the others are not held up. The first events still create the new issue and fire the alert, so the team hears about the problem long before the quota is used up.

failures.scenario: The source maps for a release were never uploaded
failures.impact: Events arrive with minified frames, producing an issue per release that nobody can read.
failures.answer: The symbolicator marks the frames as unsymbolicated and the event is stored anyway. A health check on the project says that release 4.2.1 has no maps, and the build step that deploys fails if the upload failed. When the maps arrive, stored events can be reprocessed and the duplicate issues merged.

failures.scenario: A team changes the grouping rule and every existing issue splits
failures.impact: Hundreds of old issues get duplicates, old resolved states are lost and the alerts fire again.
failures.answer: Fingerprint rules are versioned, and each event is grouped with the rule version in force when it arrived. A new rule applies to new events, and a reprocessing job can regroup history in the background, carrying over the state of the issues it merges. Teams can preview the effect on recent events before saving.

failures.scenario: Events contain passwords, tokens or personal data
failures.impact: The error service becomes a second, badly protected copy of sensitive data.
failures.answer: The SDK scrubs known fields before sending, and the server applies project rules for fields, patterns such as card numbers, and IP addresses before storing. Data is encrypted at rest and in transit, access is by role, and deleting a user's data is supported by a search on the user id.

failures.scenario: Grouping workers fall behind during a spike
failures.impact: New-issue alerts arrive late, which is the exact moment when they are needed most.
failures.answer: The queue holds the backlog and consumer lag is watched, with autoscaling on it. New fingerprints are cheap to check against a cache, so workers apply a fast path first. If the lag keeps growing, the lowest-priority work, such as sampled events from already-known hot issues, is skipped, while new fingerprints and counters keep going.

alternatives.title: How to fingerprint

options.name: Exact message
options.con: Ids and numbers in a message create thousands of issues, and different bugs with the same message merge

options.name: Exception type and in-app stack frames
options.pro: Stable across releases and across data values
options.con: Needs symbolicated frames, and refactoring a function renames the issue

options.name: Learned similarity (embeddings)
options.pro: Merges near duplicates that rules miss
options.con: Hard to explain and to debug, and costs compute per event

alternatives.pick: Stack frames by default, the normalised message when there is no stack, and custom rules for teams that need them.

alternatives.title: Where limits are enforced

options.name: In the SDK only
options.con: Cannot be trusted, and old SDK versions ignore new rules

options.name: At ingest, per project
options.pro: Protects the service and isolates projects
options.con: The data has already crossed the network

options.name: After the queue, when storing
options.pro: Smart decisions with the issue known
options.con: The queue absorbs all the load first

alternatives.pick: All three: SDK sampling to save bandwidth, a bucket at ingest to protect the service, and issue-aware sampling at storage.

alternatives.title: When to symbolicate

options.name: At ingest, before grouping
options.pro: Fingerprints use stable original names, and the stored event is readable
options.con: Extra latency and memory on the hot path, and a missing map hurts grouping

options.name: At display time
options.pro: Cheap for events nobody looks at
options.con: Grouping on minified names splits issues at every release

alternatives.pick: Before grouping, with a map cache, and fall back to the raw frames if the map is missing.

alternatives.title: How to store the events

options.name: Relational database
options.pro: Simple, and good for issues and their state
options.con: Struggles with billions of rows of events

options.name: Column store partitioned by day
options.pro: Fast aggregates and cheap retention by dropping partitions
options.con: Poor for updating single rows, so issue state lives elsewhere

alternatives.pick: A relational database for issues and state, and a column store partitioned by day for events.
